name: pain
title: Pain & Impact
description: What is hurting the buyer today, in their own words — with a quote-anchored read of how deep the pain runs (surface friction vs business metric vs personal stake), who it affects, and the consequence they attach to it as a second receipt.
prompt:
List every pain point the buyer expresses about their current situation — one entry per distinct pain. A pain point is something hurting them TODAY. A hypothetical ("it would be bad if..."), a negated statement ("we do NOT have that problem"), or a reported third-party view ("our old vendor said...") is not the buyer's pain. An empty list is correct when the buyer voiced none.

For each pain point:
- evidence: cite the buyer utterance(s), before you write "text". The quote that satisfies the layer and who_it_affects reads below must be among the quotes you cite here.
- text: the pain in the buyer's exact words — never rewritten into corporate register, never softened, no number-word/digit conversion.
- layer: how deep the pain runs, judged by what the buyer's quote actually names. surface = only a feature, task, or workflow friction is named ("the dialer drops calls"); business = the buyer names a business metric affected — revenue, cost, hours, bookings, churn, deals, headcount ("we lose two deals a week"); personal = the buyer names a personal stake — their job, their time, their stress, their reputation ("my team is drowning", "this is on me"). Choose the DEEPEST layer a quote clearly supports; when only friction is stated, it is surface, not business. Use "unclear" when no quote fixes the layer.
- who_it_affects: who the buyer says bears the pain — individual, team, department, company, customers. Assign a value only when a quote names or clearly implies the affected party; otherwise "unclear".
- quantified_impact: ONLY when the buyer states a consequence, capture it as its own receipt — evidence (the utterance) then text (the consequence in the buyer's exact words, e.g. "we lose deals every week"). Use null when the buyer states no consequence. Never infer one.

When a criterion is not clearly met, assign "unclear" rather than the more dramatic reading.
